strengths: Establishes a clean and general theoretical framework (nested tokenization, relative covering) that strictly generalizes prior byte-level lossless reduction work (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies, with rigorous proofs (Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2/3.3, Theorem 3.4) provided in the appendix.
Derives a practical, efficient top-K approximate algorithm (Algorithm 2) from the exact but expensive Algorithm 1, with clear complexity reasoning for why the nested loops can be collapsed.
Provides an illustrative worked example (Section 3.2/Appendix B) that concretely demonstrates the mechanics of the method, aiding reproducibility and understanding.

Empirical evaluation is fairly broad: multiple model families (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, Phi, Yi), multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, MMLU-Pro, and translation tasks), both greedy and temperature sampling, PoE and MoE ensembling, and an ablation over the K hyperparameter and its computational overhead.

Meaningful practical contribution: the maximal-common-vocabulary (MCV) ensemble is shown to be both more accurate/stable than heuristic baselines (Union, Naive MCV) and more computationally efficient than byte-level ensembling, addressing a genuine pain point in cross-vocabulary LLM cooperation.

Good honesty about limitations, e.g., explicit discussion that greedy decoding outputs can diverge between the original and reduced models even though the underlying text distributions are identical (Section 5.1, Appendix B).
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution, while a legitimate generalization, is somewhat incremental relative to Phan et al. (2025)/Vieira et al. (2025): the byte-level case is recovered as a special case (Vsub = A), and much of the machinery (minimal/relative covers) directly extends existing constructions.

K-LVR is only approximately lossless in practice; the paper does not provide a formal error bound or theoretical guarantee on the approximation gap introduced by the top-K truncation, relying instead on empirical closeness to the 'Full' baseline.

The construction of the maximal common vocabulary (Eq. 25) is tied specifically to BPE and to designating one tokenizer's merge rules as canonical (T1), introducing an arbitrary asymmetry between ensembled models that is not deeply analyzed; behavior with >2 models or non-BPE tokenizers (e.g., Unigram) is not empirically explored despite being mentioned as possible.

Main paper experiments are limited to a single ensemble pair (Qwen2.5-3B & Falcon3-7B) in the primary table; while more pairs appear in the appendix, the core narrative would benefit from broader main-text coverage, especially with >2 models simultaneously ensembled.

GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, and MMLU-Pro sub-sampling uses only 100 questions per category in several evaluations, which may lead to noisy accuracy estimates and limits statistical confidence in some reported deltas.

No wall-clock/throughput comparison against the naive full-vocabulary single-model baseline is given beyond the byte-level ensemble comparison, making it harder to judge the practical overhead of K-LVR relative to standard (non-ensembled) inference.

Some notational density and the layered lemma structure (Lemma 3.2/3.3, Theorem 3.4) make the paper challenging to follow without careful reading; a higher-level intuition or diagram summarizing the recursive computation earlier in Section 3 could improve accessibility.

strengths: Provides a clean and rigorous theoretical generalization of prior byte-level lossless reduction methods (Phan et al. 2025; Vieira et al. 2025) to arbitrary sub-vocabularies via the novel notion of 'nested tokenization,' with full proofs (Theorem 3.1, 3.4) and a clarifying illustrative example.
Derives a principled recursive algorithm (Algorithm 1) and a practical, efficient top-K approximation (Algorithm 2) with reasonable computational complexity analysis.

The application to ensembling models with heterogeneous vocabularies via a 'maximal common vocabulary' is a compelling and practically useful use case, showing that naive baselines (Union, Naive-MCV) can catastrophically fail while K-LVR remains robust across both PoE and MoE ensemble formulations.

Extensive empirical validation across many model families (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, Phi, Yi), multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACPBench, MMLU-Pro, WMT translation), and thorough ablations (choice of K, inference speed, vocabulary reduction consistency), which strengthens confidence in the claims.
Demonstrates measurable inference-speed advantages of MCV-based ensembling over byte-level ensembling, directly supporting the paper's efficiency motivation.
weaknesses: The practical algorithm (K-LVR) is only an approximation of the theoretically lossless procedure; no formal bound on approximation error is provided, and losslessness is only verified empirically via accuracy metrics, which may not fully capture distributional fidelity.

The construction of the maximal common vocabulary and its associated tokenizer is somewhat ad hoc (derived asymmetrically from one model's BPE merges, T1), and the paper acknowledges 'some arbitrariness' without deeply exploring alternative constructions or their impact.

Ensemble gains from MCV over simple 1-byte reduction are inconsistent and sometimes slightly worse (e.g., Table 2 MCV underperforms 1-Bytes on GSM8K and ACP; Table 6 MMLU-Pro K-LVR MCV is comparable to or barely better than the best single model), suggesting the practical benefit is efficiency rather than accuracy.

Although the introduction motivates broader applications (speculative decoding, knowledge distillation, inference-time alignment), the empirical evaluation focuses solely on ensembling; these other applications remain unvalidated.
No direct empirical comparison to the concurrent/related Hayase et al. (2025) byte-level sampling method, despite it being cited as closely related work.

The theoretical framework and notation are dense (relative coverings, nested tokenization, multiple lemmas), which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for practitioners despite the provided pseudocode.
